Creative Priming: Decoupling Process from Product to Escape the Creative Paradox

Alon Albalak    Sebastian Gabriel    David B. D’Ambrosio    Joel Lehman    Kenneth O. Stanley Email: aalbalak@lila.ai Affiliation: Lila Sciences
Abstract

Many of the most consequential advances promised by AI, from curing diseases and inventing new technologies to formulating new scientific theories, are fundamentally creative acts. Yet creativity is uniquely difficult to learn because it faces a creative paradox: learning to repeat past examples of creative success makes those specific examples more likely to recur, inhibiting the very creativity desired. This work argues that creativity is better modeled as an explicit process rather than as a property of individual artifacts, and proposes to learn the underlying generative principles behind the creative process. In particular, to escape the paradox, we introduce creative priming (CP), wherein a trained priming model generates a prompt-specific primer that assists a response model in being creative, explicitly decoupling the creative process from response generation. The priming model learns through GRPO, rewarding primers that lead to responses that are novel, high-quality, and diverse, thereby reinforcing the process that yields creative responses without reinforcing any specific response. Evaluating CP on NoveltyBench and comparing against response models directly trained for creativity, we find that priming produces a 39–200% relative increase in the number of responses that are simultaneously novel, high-quality, and semantically distinct. Additionally, although the primer is only trained to improve creativity for a small open-source model (Qwen3-8B), the creative principles it learns transfer to frontier API models, increasing the number of semantically distinct responses they generate by 4.5–10×\times and diversity by 2.5–4.6×\times, while maintaining or improving quality. CP thereby shows that decoupling the creative process from the responses themselves offers a concrete escape from the creative paradox.

 

1 Introduction

Even as benchmark after benchmark and test after test have fallen to LLMs in recent years (Rein et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2025; Patwardhan et al., 2025; Arora et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Center for AI Safety et al., 2026; Merrill et al., 2026; Sajadieh et al., 2026), creativity remains an unconquered frontier (Padmakumar and He, 2024; Sun et al., 2025; Mizrahi et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2025; Hou et al., 2026; Bao et al., 2026). Perhaps that is why many of the most compelling motivational framings for the future of AI point to creative endeavors: we will discover new cures, invent new technologies, find solutions to our most pressing problems, and imagine new art forms (Amodei, 2024; Altman, 2024). All of these looming triumphs involve fundamentally creative acts.

As AI continues to extend its dominance across an increasingly wide set of domains, the question of when this creative renaissance will begin in earnest becomes increasingly central. The focus on creativity is already reflected in scientific domains, with efforts for models to generate hypotheses, formulate research plans, anticipate scientific insights, and act as autonomous researchers (Liu et al., 2026a; Goel et al., 2025; He-Yueya et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Lupidi et al., 2026; Nathani et al., 2025). To be sure, there are some domain-specific signs of AI creativity, yet perhaps there should be more evidence after billions of dollars spent and seemingly superhuman capabilities in mathematics (Das, 2026; OpenAI, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026a). Where are the cured diseases, the revolutionary new technologies, the solutions to our energy challenges, the new genres that change the world?

Margaret Boden’s influential conception of creativity imagines a continuum from weaker to stronger forms, from the more prosaic combinatorial and exploratory creativities to the more profound transformational version (Boden, 2004). One potential hope is that models are slowly climbing this ladder as they become more generally capable, and are just now bumping against the lower rungs of transformational creativity. However, studies of scientific ideation find that model-generated ideas remain less original than human ideas and tend to stay close to familiar scientific directions (Chen et al., 2026b; Bao et al., 2026; Antoniades et al., 2026). These findings give reason to believe that creativity is unique within the intelligence landscape and cannot be learned through conventional means like other aspects of intelligence.

Consider that creativity is notoriously challenging to teach even to humans (Schooler and Melcher, 1995; Kaufman et al., 2010; Baird et al., 2012). A key obstacle is that, unlike other skills, creativity is difficult to learn from examples. While any successful past creative output could in principle serve as a training example for an aspiring student of creativity, most approaches to learning would make similar outputs more likely in the future (Jansson and Smith, 1991; Smith et al., 1993). However, for creativity, reproducing past outputs is exactly opposite the goal; rather, the goal is to learn generative principles for producing future creative outputs.

In this way, learning to be creative faces a vexing creative paradox: emulating examples of past creative success (even if they were your own successes) can actually prevent you from reaching your full creative potential. The drive to escape the past is not ideally served by reinforcing past behavior. Part of the problem is the fleeting nature of novelty; as soon as a novel artifact appears in the world, even if it was your own original idea, it is no longer novel. After all, anything in the distribution of past events is by definition not novel, which is why learning to generate past instances of novelty runs into the creative paradox.

Therefore, rather than asking what did I do that was creative, what we really want to ask is, what lessons can I abstract from the successful generation of creativity that can be reapplied to generate further creativity? Answering this question is the path to circumventing the creative paradox. The problem is that training methods do not automatically decouple the abstraction of general lessons from the reinforcement of specific past effective actions.

To address the creative paradox, this work proposes creative priming (CP), a process in which a creative priming model generates a prompt-specific creative primer (i.e. a short text) that is passed as additional context to a frozen response generation model. The priming model learns through GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), rewarding primers that lead to responses that are novel, high-quality, and diverse. Thus the system can reinforce the priming process that yields creative outputs without reinforcing any specific creative output, circumventing the creative paradox.

We evaluate CP on NoveltyBench (Zhang et al., 2025) and compare against two methods that train models to directly respond creatively. Each method is evaluated by generating 64 responses per prompt and counting the number of responses that are simultaneously novel, high-quality, and semantically distinct (a metric that we argue a creative system should score highly on), finding that CP leads to an average of 22.8 such responses per prompt, compared to 16.4 and 7.6 from direct generation methods (1.39–3.0×\times more). Furthermore, scaling the number of on-policy training samples for a direct generation baseline fails to match CP on measures of system creativity and can actually reduce performance, supporting the creative paradox’s prediction that directly reinforcing successful responses is not expected to improve creativity indefinitely. Because the primer learns general principles for creativity, it also transfers to models it was never trained with: across four API models, priming increases the number of distinct responses by 4.5–10×\times and diversity by 2.5–4.6×\times, while modestly improving quality (0.5–4.6%).

These results show that creative priming not only offers a way out of the creative paradox but can also potentially combine effectively with other techniques and even with models that were not part of the original creative priming training stack. More generally, we hope the practical gains from creative priming can help to spark deeper introspection in the field about what makes training explicitly for creativity unique compared to other kinds of learning.

2 Background

Before discussing how to improve creativity in language models, we first review what creativity is and how it can be measured. We then move on to a brief discussion of prior works on increasing creativity and why they are still vulnerable to the creative paradox.

2.1 Defining and Measuring Creativity

Definitions of human creativity often center on similar themes. For example:

  • •

    ideas that are simultaneously original and effective (Runco and Jaeger, 2012), or

  • •

    the ability to produce ideas or artifacts that are new, surprising, and valuable (Boden, 2009).

Most definitions agree that an idea must be novel and it must be good, and neither property alone is sufficient, to be called creative. Novelty, however, is nebulous without a reference point: novel to whom? Therefore, Boden (2009) also draws an essential distinction between two types of creativity: artifacts and ideas that are new to the individual who produced them (psychological creativity, or P-creativity) and those that are new in the entire history of human thought (historical creativity, or H-creativity).

Throughout this work, we study the P-creativity of language models for two reasons. First, H-creativity is nearly impossible to validate, except on a narrow set of known problems with unknown solutions that can be verified (e.g., open conjectures in math), whereas P-creativity is empirically tractable, requiring only that we have a record of a model’s previous behaviors. Second, for language models, the distinction between the two is collapsing: as frontier language models absorb ever more information, the gap between what is new to the model and what is new to humanity shrinks. For these reasons, moving forward, when we refer to creativity we are referring to P-creativity.

Mapping the requirements of Runco and Jaeger (2012) (originality and effectiveness) onto language models, originality becomes deviation, defined as the distance of a given response from some reference set of responses, and effectiveness becomes quality. Thus, the creativity of an individual response can be defined as when the response simultaneously deviates from the reference set and is high-quality. A response that departs from the reference set but is incoherent is not creative, and neither is a polished response that merely restates a common idea.

The creativity of a system can then be defined as when the system reliably produces responses that are individually creative and are also varied amongst themselves. This definition offers a direct recipe for measuring system creativity (which we will later formalize): first, remove responses that are not individually creative (i.e. those below the deviation and quality thresholds), and then measure the spread of the set that survives, so that spread is credited only among responses that are already regarded as creative.

2.2 Reinforcement Learning for Diversity

The most visible symptom of the limited creativity in modern language models is their homogeneity: across many models and even across entire model families, outputs often collapse on the same handful of ideas with only minor variations in phrasing (Jiang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). This homogeneity has motivated a wave of post-training methods to address the problem.

A number of preference-based methods formulate training data pairs to favor responses that are rare or marginally diverse while retaining quality (Chung et al., 2025; Lanchantin et al., 2025; Samuel et al., 2026), while Creative Preference Optimization incorporates novelty, diversity, surprise, and quality directly into preference optimization (Ismayilzada et al., 2025). Other methods instead construct rewards from collections of generated responses, using learned semantic partitions in DARLING (Li et al., 2025), determinantal point processes in Diversity Quality Optimization (Chen et al., 2026a), or specialization across a vector-valued reward space in Vector Policy Optimization (Bahlous-Boldi et al., 2026). CreativeInstruct takes a complementary instruction-tuning approach, teaching the response model when to enter creativity-biased spans (Sahu et al., 2026). In this work, two families of diversity-enhancing methods that differ only in how they measure diversity serve as baselines. Both methods train the response model to directly respond to prompts (top in Figure 1) with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024).

2.2.1 Group-Relative Policy Optimization

In GRPO, for each prompt XX, a group of GG responses {Y1,…,YG}\{Y_{1},\dots,Y_{G}\} is sampled from the model, Y∼π(⋅∣X)Y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid X), and each response is scored with a reward rir_{i}, forming a group-relative advantage,

Ai=ri−mean⁡({r1,…,rG})std⁡({r1,…,rG}).A_{i}=\frac{r_{i}-\mathrm{mean}(\{r_{1},\dots,r_{G}\})}{\mathrm{std}(\{r_{1},\dots,r_{G}\})}. (1)

In this work, all models are trained with GRPO as the backbone and vary only in how the reward rir_{i} is defined. Throughout, let ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot) be an embedding model and let d⁡(a,b)=min⁡(1, 1−cos⁡θa​b)∈[0,1]\mathrm{d}(a,b)=\min\!\big(1,\,1-\cos\theta_{ab}\big)\in[0,1] denote the cosine distance between two responses, where θa​b=∠⁡(ϕ⁡(a),ϕ⁡(b))\theta_{ab}=\angle(\phi(a),\phi(b)) is the angle between their embeddings.

2.2.2 Diversity-Enhancing Baselines

We consider two families of diversity-enhancing methods that differ only in how they measure diversity. Both methods train the response model to directly respond to prompts (top in Figure 1).

Diversified GRPO (DGRPO).

The first method, Diversified GRPO (DGRPO), inspired by Diversified DPO and Diversified ORPO (Chung et al., 2025), recasts their objective as a PPO-style algorithm, trading their labeled preference data (expensive and limiting to collect) for on-policy sampling. DGRPO rewards each response by the product of its quality QiQ_{i} and its intra-group diversity DiD_{i},

ri=Qi⋅Di,Di=1G−1​∑j≠id⁡(Yi,Yj),Qi=σ⁡((rRM​(X,Yi)−T)/τ).r_{i}=Q_{i}\cdot D_{i},\qquad D_{i}=\frac{1}{G-1}\sum_{j\neq i}\mathrm{d}(Y_{i},Y_{j}),\qquad Q_{i}=\sigma\!\big((r_{\mathrm{RM}}(X,Y_{i})-T)/\tau\big). (2)

The quality term is a reward-model score passed through a logistic gate with threshold TT and temperature τ\tau, while diversity is the response’s mean cosine distance from the other responses in its sampled group. Exact definitions and the complete training loop are in Appendix A.3.

Partition-based diversity (DARLING).

The second method, Diversity-Aware Reinforcement Learning (DARLING) (Li et al., 2025), replaces QiQ_{i} with the raw reward-model quality score, and DiD_{i} with a partition-based signal. For the parition-based diversity, a learned equivalence classifier groups the GG responses into semantic partitions, and YiY_{i} is rewarded in proportion to how many of its peers are distinct from it, Di=(G−|partition⁡(i)|)/(G−1)D_{i}=(G-|\mathrm{partition}(i)|)\,/\,(G-1), so that responses in rare partitions score highest. The potential benefit of DARLING over DGRPO lies in the learned equivalence classifier; it is trained to measure diversity beyond surface-level lexical variations.

3 Approach: Creative Priming

Rather than directly optimizing the response model to be creative, creative priming (CP) treats creativity as a process and decouples abstract thinking from response generation, training a separate policy that learns to guide a frozen response model.

A creative primer is a short text YCPY_{\mathrm{CP}} produced by the creative priming policy πCP\pi_{\mathrm{CP}} that is conditioned on the original prompt XX. The primer combines with XX through a prompt template 𝒯⁡(⋅,⋅)\mathcal{T}(\cdot,\cdot) and feeds into the response model πresp\pi_{\mathrm{resp}} (Figure 1 and Eq 3; an example of 𝒯\mathcal{T} is later provided in Figure 15 of the Appendix). In creative priming, only πCP\pi_{\mathrm{CP}} is trained while the response model πresp\pi_{\mathrm{resp}} is frozen. A response is thus generated in a two-stage process,

YCP∼πCP(⋅∣X),Yresp∼πresp(⋅∣𝒯(X,YCP)),Y_{\mathrm{CP}}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{CP}}(\cdot\mid X),\qquad Y_{\mathrm{resp}}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{resp}}\!\big(\cdot\mid\mathcal{T}(X,Y_{\mathrm{CP}})\big), (3)

so that πCP\pi_{\mathrm{CP}} steers the response only through the primer YCPY_{\mathrm{CP}}.

3.1 Algorithm

Training applies Equation 3 as a 2-step pipeline: for each prompt XjX^{j} we sample a group of GCPG_{\mathrm{CP}} primers, and for each primer YCPj,iY_{\mathrm{CP}}^{j,i} we sample a group of GrespG_{\mathrm{resp}} responses,

{YCPj,i}i=1GCP∼πCP(⋅∣Xj),{Yrespj,i,k}k=1Gresp∼πresp(⋅∣𝒯(Xj,YCPj,i)),\{Y_{\mathrm{CP}}^{j,i}\}_{i=1}^{G_{\mathrm{CP}}}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{CP}}(\cdot\mid X^{j}),\qquad\{Y_{\mathrm{resp}}^{j,i,k}\}_{k=1}^{G_{\mathrm{resp}}}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{resp}}\!\big(\cdot\mid\mathcal{T}(X^{j},Y_{\mathrm{CP}}^{j,i})\big), (4)

so that the rewards can score each primer YCPj,iY_{\mathrm{CP}}^{j,i} based on the creativity of the GrespG_{\mathrm{resp}} responses it induces.

Each creative primer YCPj,iY_{\mathrm{CP}}^{j,i} receives a scalar reward rj,i=Reward⁡(⋅)r_{j,i}=\mathrm{Reward}(\cdot), whose group-level advantage across the GCPG_{\mathrm{CP}} primers is calculated as typical for GRPO (Eq. 1). We optimize πCP\pi_{\mathrm{CP}} with the resulting clipped GRPO objective and a KL penalty to a reference policy. The full training loop is given in Algorithm 2 in the appendix.

3.2 Reward Components

The primer reward is a product of signals at two levels: response-level signals that measure the creativity of the responses a primer induces, and primer-level signals that regularize the primer model itself:

Reward=C⋅Dintra⋅Dinter⏟response-level (creativity)⋅JCP⋅DintraCP⋅DinterCP⏟primer-level (regularizers)\mathrm{Reward}=\;\underbrace{C\cdot D_{\mathrm{intra}}\cdot D_{\mathrm{inter}}}_{\text{response-level (creativity)}}\;\cdot\;\underbrace{J_{\mathrm{CP}}\cdot D^{\mathrm{CP}}_{\mathrm{intra}}\cdot D^{\mathrm{CP}}_{\mathrm{inter}}}_{\text{primer-level (regularizers)}} (5)

Rewards are multiplied rather than summed so that a primer scores well only when every signal is simultaneously high. Every signal occupies the same [0,1][0,1] range to normalize the impact of each factor.

Notation.

The components discussed in this section reuse the embedding model ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot) and cosine distance d⁡(a,b)\mathrm{d}(a,b) from Section 2.2.1. For the primer under consideration, its GrespG_{\mathrm{resp}} responses are {Yrespj,i,k}k=1Gresp\{Y_{\mathrm{resp}}^{j,i,k}\}_{k=1}^{G_{\mathrm{resp}}}, and let ℛref={Yrefj,k}k=1Gresp\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{ref}}=\{Y_{\mathrm{ref}}^{j,k}\}_{k=1}^{G_{\mathrm{resp}}} be the GrespG_{\mathrm{resp}} reference responses for the same prompt.

3.2.1 Response-level signals

The three response-level signals measure the creativity of the response set a primer induces, following the definition adopted in Section 2.1, through each response’s individual creativity and the variety of the set as a whole.

Response creativity CC.

Following the convention in Section 2.1 that an individual response is creative when it is simultaneously deviating and high-quality, each response’s individual-response creativity is scored by multiplying its deviation with its quality and then averaged over the group. The deviation of response kk is its mean distance to the reference set (Figure 2),

Devk=1Gresp​∑Yref∈ℛrefd⁡(Yrespj,i,k,Yref).\mathrm{Dev}_{k}=\frac{1}{G_{\mathrm{resp}}}\sum_{Y_{\mathrm{ref}}\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{ref}}}\mathrm{d}\!\left(Y_{\mathrm{resp}}^{j,i,k},Y_{\mathrm{ref}}\right). (6)

Let qk=rRM​(Xj,Yrespj,i,k)q_{k}=r_{\mathrm{RM}}\!\left(X^{j},Y_{\mathrm{resp}}^{j,i,k}\right) be the raw reward-model score of response kk, scored against the original prompt XjX^{j} (without the primer). Then the individual-response creativity of response kk multiplies its deviation with its normalized quality,

ck=Devk⋅σ⁡(qk−Tτ),c_{k}=\mathrm{Dev}_{k}\cdot\sigma\!\left(\frac{q_{k}-T}{\tau}\right), (7)

where σ\sigma is the logistic sigmoid, TT is the reward-model threshold, and τ>0\tau>0 is a temperature controlling the sharpness of the sigmoid. The response creativity of primer YC​Pj,iY^{j,i}_{CP} is then the mean of these per-response scores over the group it induces,

C=1Gresp​∑k=1Grespck.C=\frac{1}{G_{\mathrm{resp}}}\sum_{k=1}^{G_{\mathrm{resp}}}c_{k}. (8)

We also experiment with training the creative priming model without deviation, as discussed in Section 3.3, in which case CC reduces to a quality-only signal, given in Appendix A.2.

Intra-group diversity.

DintraD_{\mathrm{intra}}, the mean pairwise cosine distance among the responses from a single creative primer YC​Pj,iY^{j,i}_{CP}, rewards primers that lead to increased response diversity:

Dintra=1(Gresp2)​∑k=1Gresp∑k′=k+1Grespd⁡(Yrespj,i,k,Yrespj,i,k′).D_{\mathrm{intra}}=\frac{1}{\binom{G_{\mathrm{resp}}}{2}}\sum_{k=1}^{G_{\mathrm{resp}}}\sum_{k^{\prime}=k+1}^{G_{\mathrm{resp}}}\mathrm{d}\!\left(Y_{\mathrm{resp}}^{j,i,k},Y_{\mathrm{resp}}^{j,i,k^{\prime}}\right). (9)
Inter-group diversity.

DinterD_{\mathrm{inter}}, the mean distance from YC​Pj,iY^{j,i}_{CP}’s responses to the responses of other primers to the same prompt XjX^{j}, rewards primers that lead to responses which deviate from other primer’s responses:

Dinter=1(GCP−1)​Gresp2​∑k=1Gresp∑i′≠i∑k′=1Grespd⁡(Yrespj,i,k,Yrespj,i′,k′).D_{\mathrm{inter}}=\frac{1}{(G_{\mathrm{CP}}-1)\,G_{\mathrm{resp}}^{2}}\sum_{k=1}^{G_{\mathrm{resp}}}\sum_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\sum_{k^{\prime}=1}^{G_{\mathrm{resp}}}\mathrm{d}\!\left(Y_{\mathrm{resp}}^{j,i,k},Y_{\mathrm{resp}}^{j,i^{\prime},k^{\prime}}\right). (10)

3.2.2 Primer-level signals

The remaining three signals act on the primers directly and their main purpose is to regularize and diversify the primer model: they keep primers high-quality and specific to each prompt.

Creative primer judge JCPJ_{\mathrm{CP}}.

An LLM-as-a-judge scores the primer YCPj,iY_{\mathrm{CP}}^{j,i} on a set of five criteria 𝒥={\mathcal{J}=\{specificity, thinking strategy, content focus, prompt faithfulness, focus}\}, each in [0,100][0,100]. The judge score is the mean of these criteria, but is set to zero if the primer refers to the response model in the third person rather than addressing it directly:

JCP=𝟙direct⋅1100​|𝒥|∑c∈𝒥sc.J_{\mathrm{CP}}=\mathds{1}_{\text{direct}}\cdot\frac{1}{100\,|\mathcal{J}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{J}}s_{c}. (11)

The prompt template is included in Figure 16. We also experimented with a penalty-based rubric that instead subtracts weighted penalties for specific failure modes, defined and evaluated in Appendix B.

Creative primer intra-prompt diversity DintraCPD^{\mathrm{CP}}_{\mathrm{intra}}.

This measure weighs diversity among the creative primers produced for the same prompt XjX^{j}, encouraging diversity amongst the primers themselves. For primer YC​Pj,iY^{j,i}_{CP}:

DintraCP=1GCP−1​∑i′≠id⁡(YCPj,i,YCPj,i′).D^{\mathrm{CP}}_{\mathrm{intra}}=\frac{1}{G_{\mathrm{CP}}-1}\sum_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\mathrm{d}\!\left(Y_{\mathrm{CP}}^{j,i},Y_{\mathrm{CP}}^{j,i^{\prime}}\right). (12)
Creative primer inter-prompt diversity DinterCPD^{\mathrm{CP}}_{\mathrm{inter}}.

This measure of diversity is the mean distance between a creative primer generated for prompt jj, YC​Pj,iY^{j,i}_{CP}, and every primer generated for a different prompt j′j^{\prime} in the batch of BB prompts, which rewards the primer model for tailoring its primers to each prompt rather than reusing a single generic primer:

DinterCP=1(B−1)​GCP​∑j′≠j∑i′=1GCPd⁡(YCPj,i,YCPj′,i′).D^{\mathrm{CP}}_{\mathrm{inter}}=\frac{1}{(B-1)\,G_{\mathrm{CP}}}\sum_{j^{\prime}\neq j}\sum_{i^{\prime}=1}^{G_{\mathrm{CP}}}\mathrm{d}\!\left(Y_{\mathrm{CP}}^{j,i},Y_{\mathrm{CP}}^{j^{\prime},i^{\prime}}\right). (13)

3.3 Learning the Creative Process

Training only the primer model while keeping the response model frozen explicitly decouples learning the abstract creative procedure from producing responses, and is thereby crucial to avoiding the creative paradox. Typically, in diversity-enhancing RL, the response model is directly rewarded for producing specific outputs. However, because πCP\pi_{\mathrm{CP}} is only rewarded for inducing better responses in a separate model, it is never directly rewarded for reproducing past outputs. It is therefore free to learn generative principles for creativity rather than to reinforce what already worked, which is how it escapes the creative paradox. Decoupling the creative procedure from generating responses also makes the method modular, such that a single trained πCP\pi_{\mathrm{CP}} can potentially be trained on a small πresp\pi_{\mathrm{resp}} but transferred to a larger, more capable model at inference time.

4 Experimental Setup

The aim of the experimental approach is to provide a multifaceted view of the potential advantages of creative priming relative to baselines and other creativity-enhancing methods through a number of measures and perspectives.

Models.

In these experiments all creative priming models πCP\pi_{\mathrm{CP}} and, unless otherwise noted, all response models πresp\pi_{\mathrm{resp}} are Qwen3-8B (Team, 2025). Several targeted models calculate rewards during training: quality is scored by the Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.1-8B reward model, diversity and deviation are calculated from embeddings of the Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B model, DARLING’s partition signal depends on a ModernBERT similarity classifier11 1 https://huggingface.co/dogtooth/similarity-classifier-f168-hf, and the creative primer judge is Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct.

Training data.

All methods are trained on a filtered subset of Infinite-Chats22 2 https://huggingface.co/datasets/LilaSciences/infinite-chats-scored (Jiang et al., 2025) (which is itself a subset of WildChat from Zhao et al., 2024). To create this subset, an LLM judge scores each prompt’s suitability along three axes: open-endedness, complexity, and creative potential. Each axis is rated on a 0–3 scale, and only prompts with a combined score ≥6\geq 6 are retained, yielding 21,075 prompts. Additionally, when training creative priming models, a pool of 32 custom-written creative primer prompt templates wrap the prompts before they are passed to the priming model. The reference set for calculating deviation consists of eight responses per prompt from the initial model checkpoint.

Evaluation data.

The evaluation dataset is NoveltyBench (Zhang et al., 2025), which includes 100 real-world open-ended prompts intended to elicit creativity. To measure quality, the original dataset is extended so that each prompt comes with an LLM judge prompt with two families of components: six universal components fixed across all prompts (instruction-following, coherence, completeness, conciseness, clarity, and surprise), and an additional 1–3 prompt-specific components generated by claude-opus-4-20250514. For example, “Tell me a story in five sentences about a girl and her dog” has 2 prompt-specific components: emotional resonance and narrative economy. The judge prompt template is in Figure 17 in Appendix K. The evaluation set, including the judge prompts, is available on the HuggingFace Hub.33 3 https://huggingface.co/datasets/LilaSciences/novelty-bench-llm-judge Evaluation uses the creative primer prompt template in Figure 14 in Appendix K.

Baselines.

Four baselines provide comparisons to creative priming: (1) direct generation from the initial Qwen3-8B checkpoint; (2) an untrained creative priming model; (3) Diversified GRPO (DGRPO), which trains the response model directly with a multiplicative quality ×\times intra-group cosine-distance diversity reward; and (4) DARLING (Li et al., 2025), which replaces the embedding diversity with a partition-based diversity signal. Because deviation is a direct component of creativity metrics, in addition to their original formulations, we train both DGRPO and DARLING with and without an added deviation reward to isolate its effect.

Training hyperparameters.

When training models, the group sizes are GCP=8G_{\mathrm{CP}}=8 primers per prompt and G=8G=8 responses per prompt for DGRPO and DARLING, so that each policy’s group-relative advantage is estimated on the same number of on-policy samples per prompt. Additionally, to estimate rewards for each primer, Gresp=8G_{\mathrm{resp}}=8 responses are generated per primer (and their scores averaged as described in Section 3.2). CP and DGRPO train for two epochs with a batch size of 256, a learning rate of 1×10−61\times 10^{-6}, temperature 1.01.0 with top-pp 0.90.9, the quality gate is at threshold T=−5.0T=-5.0, and sigmoid temperature τ=1.0\tau=1.0. The DARLING model is trained with the same hyperparameters from the original paper, including training for ten epochs (Li et al., 2025). In effect, to be faithful to its original setup, DARLING receives 5 times more epochs than CP or DGRPO.

Evaluation hyperparameters.

To evaluate the baselines and CP models, n=64n=64 completions are generated per prompt with temperature 1.01.0, top-pp 1.01.0, and a maximum of 44,096096 generated tokens. Qwen3’s thinking mode is left enabled and the thinking span is stripped before scoring, so that every metric is computed on the answers alone. For CP methods, 1 response is generated per primer, meaning that 64 primers are generated, each separately used as input for 1 response.

Evaluation metrics.

This evaluation reports five atomic metrics, each isolating a single characteristic of a method, before combining them into compound measures of system-level creativity.

Quality and deviation are the two axes along which an individual response is measured for creativity, whereas diversity, Vendi score, and distinct clusters measure the spread of a response set. Quality is scored by Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 using the prompt-specific judge template shown in Figure 17 in Appendix K. Deviation is the distance to the closest of 64 direct-generation reference responses. That is, the mean operator from training (Eq. 6) is replaced with a minimum operator so that during evaluation the worst-case nearest neighbor distance is measured. Diversity is the mean pairwise cosine distance within a response set (Eq. 9). Vendi score is an information-theoretic measure of the number of distinct responses in a set (Friedman and Dieng, 2023). Distinct clusters counts the semantic-equivalence clusters in a set, following NoveltyBench (Zhang et al., 2025), using the partition model at yimingzhang/deberta-v3-large-generation-similarity. Deviation, diversity, and Vendi score use embeddings from jinaai/jina-embeddings-v5-text-small, deliberately different than the embedding model from training to avoid overfitting to a specific model.

Whereas each atomic metric isolates one characteristic, the compound metrics combine them to capture system-level creativity, i.e. the ability to reliably produce a variety of individually creative responses. Each compound metric therefore first discards non-creative responses (responses failing a quality or deviation threshold) and then measures the spread of the survivors using filtered Vendi score and filtered distinct clusters, so that spread is credited only among responses already deemed creative. However, the optimal threshold varies based on the application, so we additionally sweep the thresholds across their full range. Sweeping the deviation (or quality) threshold and integrating over that sweep yields an area under the curve (AUC-dev or AUC-qual) that summarizes the method’s filtered Vendi score or distinct clusters across all thresholds. A comprehensive system-level creativity metric can accordingly be formulated through computing the volume under the deviation ×\times quality surface (VUS) by jointly sweeping thresholds over both metrics. Default thresholds and further metric details are detailed in Appendix C.

Scaling experiment.

In addition to the primary experimental settings above, a further evaluation of the creative paradox is performed by scaling the number of on-policy training samples in DGRPO: if directly reinforcing successful responses limits creativity, then reinforcing more responses should not continually improve system-level creativity. Accordingly, in this experiment DGRPO (with divergence) is trained with group sizes G∈{8,16,32,64}G\in\{8,16,32,64\}. At the lower endpoint, G=8G=8, DGRPO matches CP’s eight on-policy primers per prompt, as in the primary setup. However, the reward of each primer for CP is estimated by averaging across eight responses, so at G=64G=64 DGRPO instead matches the total number of responses per prompt for CP, but gets the advantage of eight times more on-policy samples. The scaling study focuses on DGRPO because DARLING already trains for five times more epochs than CP and DGRPO.

5 Findings & Analysis

The main results in Table 1 are split among untrained methods (top rows), methods trained without a deviation term (middle rows), and methods trained with deviation (bottom rows). Results on atomic metrics are on the left and compound metrics, which aggregate the atomic metrics in various ways, are on the right. For presentation purposes only, we represent diversity and deviation as scores out of 100100. Figure 3 shows one qualitative example output for each method, including the primer that CP produced, with further examples in Appendix G.

Performance at first glance.

The atomic metrics suggest that every method trades one property for another, differing only in how steep the tradeoff is. For example, within the models trained for quality and diversity (middle rows), DGRPO improves diversity (2626), Vendi score (4.364.36), and distinct clusters (37.137.1) over the reference, at a slight cost to quality (90.5→87.590.5\to 87.5). DARLING makes the opposite trade, achieving the highest quality of any method (93.693.6) while its diversity (11.711.7) falls slightly below the reference (12.312.3), and its Vendi score and distinct clusters barely move (2.172.17 and 20.520.5). CP makes the same tradeoff, but on more favorable terms, losing only a little quality (90.5→88.290.5\to 88.2) in return for the highest diversity (31.231.2), deviation (21.221.2), Vendi score (5.395.39), and distinct clusters (39.539.5) of any method not trained with deviation.

Adding deviation to the reward signal increases the deviation score for all three trained methods, but they respond very differently. DGRPO improves significantly in diversity (26→3426\to 34), but the quality (87.5→77.387.5\to 77.3) and number of distinct clusters decrease (37.1→33.437.1\to 33.4). DARLING also enjoys significant improvement in diversity (11.7→1811.7\to 18) and the number of distinct clusters (20.5→28.120.5\to 28.1), but drops some quality (93.6→88.493.6\to 88.4). CP also loses quality (88.2→85.788.2\to 85.7), but with less tradeoff than DGRPO and DARLING, in return for the most distinct clusters of any method (45.345.3), while holding diversity and deviation high.

The creative paradox, measured.

The atomic metrics from above, however, do not tell us whether an individual response is creative (simultaneously deviating and high-quality), nor whether a system is creative (generates a large spread of creative responses). The compound metrics directly capture the joint demands of creativity by filtering out individual responses that are not creative and then measuring the spread of the remaining responses, which is where the difference between CP and the baseline approaches becomes evident.

Among the methods trained without deviation, DARLING has high-quality but low-diversity responses, so its filtered Vendi (0.570.57) and filtered distinct clusters (1.761.76) are the lowest in the block. DGRPO is the opposite, producing almost as many distinct clusters as CP (37.137.1 and 39.539.5); however, most responses fall below the quality or deviation threshold and are filtered out, dropping its filtered distinct clusters to just 6.026.02. Compared to the baselines, CP leads to better performance on both filtered metrics (4.044.04 filtered Vendi and 16.116.1 filtered distinct clusters) and on metrics that sweep across all threshold values (AUC-dev, AUC-qual, and VUS in Table 1). None of these results mean that the baselines are failing: each performs well on its intended objective, but neither achieve the simultaneous deviation, quality, and diversity expected of a creative system.

Deviation is a core ingredient of what makes a response, and thus a system, creative. However, even when the baselines are trained with an explicit deviation reward, they do not outperform a CP model trained without deviation on the compound metrics. On filtered Vendi, CP without deviation (4.044.04) already exceeds both DGRPO (2.852.85) and DARLING (2.62.6) trained with deviation. Filtered distinct clusters tell the same story: CP without deviation (16.116.1) stays well ahead of DGRPO (7.597.59) and draws even with DARLING (16.416.4), the strongest baseline. That CP does so even without explicitly optimizating for deviation suggests that optimizing for the individual components of creativity only goes so far, and that learning the creative process does more to drive creativity (Section 3.3).

One might expect that direct generation methods should improve on metrics of creativity when trained with a larger group size, as more on-policy samples give a model more opportunities to explore and to reinforce high-reward responses. However, interestingly, scaling the number of on-policy samples for DGRPO trained with deviation does not allow it to escape the tradeoff observed above (DGRPO is evaluated here instead of DARLING because it performs better on a majority of compound metrics while training for 5 times fewer epochs). Compared to the reference model, at G=8G=8, DGRPO already gains diversity and deviation at the cost of quality, and Figure 4(a) shows that increasing group sizes to G∈{16,32,64}G\in\{16,32,64\} does not resolve the tradeoffs, but can actually further exaggerate them. As GG increases, deviation is the only metric that rises consistently, increasing from 25.625.6 to 33.533.5. Diversity and Vendi score decline steadily, while quality and distinct clusters fluctuate before reaching their lowest values at G=64G=64 (69.169.1 and 24.524.5, respectively).

The compound metrics reveal the consequences of this tradeoff (Figure 4(b), with full results in Appendix H), where at G=32G=32, empirically the best group size, DGRPO still has worse performance than CP on every compound metric. At best, DGRPO with G=32G=32 achieves 93.4% of the VUS-Vendi that CP achieves, and at worst, only 65.2% of the AUC-dev distinct clusters. Ultimately, at G=64G=64 every metric of system creativity decreases from the peak. Even though scaling up to G=64G=64 gives DGRPO a compute advantage versus lower values of GG, that additional compute neither closes the gap nor produces continual improvements in creativity, providing intriguing further evidence for the creative paradox: directly reinforcing successful responses can improve creativity only up to a point, after which reinforcing more responses begins to undermine system-level creativity.

Decomposing the Creative Priming advantage.

To disentangle the contributions of the priming process, RL training, and the deviation reward, we compare three CP variants. If Qwen3-8B serves as the creative primer without any additional RL (the untrained CP row), diversity already increases from 12.312.3 to 20.620.6 over direct generation while judged quality stays flat (91.791.7 versus 90.590.5). However, the CP model trained with quality and diversity still dominates the untrained variant on nearly every metric (with a minor decrease in quality). Further including the deviation reward improves the creativity metrics still further, at an additional small cost to quality. This analysis shows that the creative priming process is valuable on its own, but RL training delivers significant additional gains; the process supplies a mechanism by which creativity can emerge, and training teaches the model to optimize that mechanism.

The learned creative process transfers to frontier models.

The creative priming model is only trained with a Qwen3-8B response model, so it is natural to consider that it may overfit to that model. We test whether the learned creative process transfers by pairing trained CP models with four unseen response models (Claude Sonnet-4.6, Claude Opus-4.8, GPT-5-nano, and GPT-5.4), evaluating each against its own direct-generation reference. Across all four API models, CP increases diversity by 2.52.5–4.6×4.6\times and distinct clusters by 4.54.5–10×10\times while maintaining or improving quality (Figure 5). For example, with Sonnet-4.6, distinct clusters increase from 2.82.8 to 28.528.5 and diversity from 5.35.3 to 24.624.6, while quality also increases from 90.290.2 to 94.394.3. In this way, the evidence suggests that the learned process effectively improves the atomic metrics of response models unseen during training.

We next evaluate whether the learned process also elicits an increase in system-level creativity metrics from each API model. Because each response model is evaluated against its own direct-generation reference, the compound metrics are model-relative: they measure whether CP leads to varied responses that depart from what that model typically generates while meeting its own quality threshold. Accordingly, these creativity scores cannot be directly compared across response models. Table 4 in Appendix D shows that the deviation-trained CP model achieves filtered Vendi scores ranging from 3.263.26–4.714.71 and filtered distinct scores of 10.410.4–21.921.9 across the four API models. For context, CP paired with Qwen3-8B achieves a filtered Vendi score of 4.704.70 and a filtered distinct score of 22.822.8, falling within a similar range as the API models. For the API models, VUS Vendi ranges from 112.8112.8–177.7177.7, and VUS distinct clusters are 395.3395.3–822.7822.7. Notably, while creative priming elicits the highest creativity scores when paired with GPT-5.4 and GPT-5-nano, it achieves the lowest creativity scores when paired with Opus-4.8. This is possibly due to Opus-4.8 having the highest quality scores from its direct response baseline (91.791.7), combined with the lowest deviation scores from the CP model (17.117.1). Table 4 in Appendix D reports the complete results.

Modularity in the creative priming pipeline.

The previous experiment varies the response model, but the creative priming pipeline also permits varying the creative priming model. We evaluate filtered Vendi scores across the full cross-product of {creative priming model ×\times response model} pairs, drawing both roles from the deviation-trained baselines, a trained CP model, and an untrained Qwen3-8B prompted as a primer (Figure 6). The main result of this analysis is that the priming pipeline itself improves every response model over direct generation. Specifically, the trained CP model is the best primer of the group, giving the three highest-scoring cells of the grid (4.1534.153–4.9914.991). However, even DGRPO and DARLING work well as primers: used to prime the initial Qwen3-8B (top row of Figure 6), they reach 2.7922.792 and 3.223.22, well above the untrained primer (1.4801.480), despite never being trained to prime another model.

The quality-deviation frontier.

Given that models exhibit an inherent trade-off between quality and deviation, it is interesting to measure the Pareto-frontier share of each method on the quality-deviation frontier, a measure of how well a method handles that trade-off. To capture this trade-off, each response is plotted on a quality-deviation chart (separately for each evaluation prompt) with the Pareto frontier (the non-dominated responses) highlighted, and the percent of the frontier composed of each method’s responses is then calculated. Figure 7 shows an example of this approach for one prompt. Finally, the scores are averaged across all prompts, measuring how often each method produces responses that dominate the competitors on quality and deviation jointly. Because each frontier is relative to the pool of competing methods, we compute the share within each pool (with and without deviation), where it sums to 100%. Table 2 reports these shares.

CP claims the majority of the frontier both with and without deviation, and by a wide margin without deviation (72.6%). This trend holds even where CP tops neither raw quality or deviation: among the deviation-trained methods it leads neither deviation nor quality alone, yet it still contributes the largest share of jointly non-dominated responses (45.3%45.3\%).

A consistent picture.

Where the baselines re-tread the creative paradox by training on their own past successes, CP is built to escape it—and the results bear this out, with CP substantially outperforming the baselines as a creative system. This trend holds regardless of how we look: the filtered compound metrics, the threshold-free sweeps, transfer across frozen response models, and variation of the primer model itself all tell the same story. We turn next to the broader implications of these results.

6 Discussion

A major implication of the creative paradox, along with the effectiveness of creative priming, is that the “normal way” of thinking about machine learning may not ultimately work as well for creativity. In the normal framing, a model learns from examples of good behavior and gradually improves at reproducing such behavior. Creativity upends this intuitive notion by offering a case where you actually do not want future behavior to resemble past behavior. Or, to be more nuanced about the precise challenge: there is one sense in which we definitively do not want the output to resemble the training while there is another sense in which we do. On the one hand, the products of creative generation themselves should diverge from their precedent in training, while on the other hand the process behind those generations should follow shared principles. The problem is that the underlying process is generally not in the training data and, even if it were, it would need to be separated from the products it led to. The creative paradox emerges from this delicate conflict.

The main hypothesis behind creative priming is therefore that creativity does not live in individual input/output pairs but in the process that generates them. Four results support this view:

  1. 1.

    Table 1 shows that even a deviation-less CP model improves on compound creativity metrics compared to baselines that are explicitly trained to deviate from past responses;

  2. 2.

    Figure 4 shows that increasing training compute for direct generation hits a peak performance which, by all measures of system creativity, is worse than CP;

  3. 3.

    Figure 5 shows that the creative process learned by the priming model on a small open-source response model transfers to frontier API response models, leading to a 4.5-10×\times increase in the number of distinct responses and a 2.5-4.6×\times increase in response diversity; and

  4. 4.

    Figure 6 shows that the priming process itself improves response models even when the model generating the primer was not trained for priming.

All these results point to a learned procedure that need not reinforce any particular output and does not depend critically upon any particular response model. Avoiding the creative paradox thus requires learning the generative principle behind creative successes rather than learning to reproduce those same successes reliably.

A key facet of creative priming is decoupling priming from response generation. How critical is such a decoupling? When a response model is optimized directly, the components of creativity trade off against one another: DGRPO increases diversity and deviation by sacrificing quality, while DARLING protects quality at the expense of diversity. Furthermore, additional compute does not break this trade-off for DGRPO: deviation consistently improves with increasing group sizes, but the other atomic metrics ultimately decline, leading to a creativity ceiling that scale does not fix. Decoupling the priming from the response softens this trade-off. The response model keeps doing exactly what it is trained for, producing the highest-quality answer, while the primer supplies the shift toward diverse regions of the output distribution, so neither objective is compromised for the other. This division of labor is how the primer ultimately learns creative principles rather than to reproduce high-quality answers itself.

Additional evidence to support decoupling relates to style versus substance. If a method genuinely increases creativity, it should change the content of the responses more than the surface-level style. While experiments in Appendix F show that all three methods change style relative to the reference, CP drifts least from the reference response model’s style, exhibiting the lowest function-word JS-divergence of the three (0.045, where lower means closer to matching the reference’s style, compared with DGRPO’s 0.087 and DARLING’s 0.138). Decoupling predicts precisely such consistency. The primer steers content, whereas training the response model directly entangles the content changes with a larger stylistic shift. Figure 3 shows a qualitative example of the style differences.

A natural question is whether a single model could internalize the creative priming process and use it within its chain-of-thought. The obstacle to this more straightforward approach is that models are trained toward the highest-quality response. As a result, it is unlikely that one model captures the full distribution of high quality outputs with enough likelihood to also be reliably diverse. That limitation is exactly what the primer exploits. Modifying the response model’s prompt pushes it into a different region of the input distribution and elicits a shifted output distribution, so the primer is a learned, external way to induce the shift rather than asking one model to be simultaneously quality-maximizing and distribution-covering. Nevertheless, in principle perhaps there is a way for a single model to write the primer for itself and then respond to it, so long as priming stays a separate stage. Folding creative priming into a single model is an interesting direction for future investigation.

An intriguing benefit of the separated primer in this paper is that it is modular and can be trained once and reused, i.e. swapped across response models or even moved to a new domain by pairing it with a domain-specific response model. Furthermore, priming can be combined with most test-time diversity-enhancing methods, including sequential sampling (Kang and Zhang, 2025), String Seed of Thought (Misaki and Akiba, 2026), vector policy optimization (Bahlous-Boldi et al., 2026), verbalized sampling (Zhang et al., 2026) as shown in Appendix E, or, as shown in Figure 6, a diversity-trained response model.

In Section 2.1, a response was defined as being creative when it “simultaneously deviates from the reference set and is high-quality” and a system was defined as creative “when the system reliably produces responses that are individually creative and are also varied amongst themselves.” An important consequence of these definitions is obvious in hindsight: the moment a model produces an idea, it is, by definition, no longer new to that model. Novelty is spent in the very act of its creation. Creativity is thus not a fixed property of any single output, but an ongoing process of repeatedly generating original, high-quality ideas. In this work, the reference set from the response model was frozen prior to training, enabling a comparable computation of deviation for all methods. Looking ahead, there is room for a richer, and more complex, measurement that allows for a non-stationary reference set. By computing deviation against the full history of a model’s outputs, the temporal dimension of creativity can be directly captured: instead of a snapshot of creativity at one instant, a system can be evaluated for the ability to sustain novelty against its own growing past history. However, such a measurement makes comparisons more complicated because each system, even for two runs of the same method, will accumulate their own distinct reference sets.

Limitations.

One obvious downside of the creative priming pipeline is that two-stage generation adds additional inference cost over direct generation. Additionally, the priming pipeline is bounded by the frozen response model: it can only elicit what the response model is already capable of producing and lacks any means to add knowledge or skill that the response model does not already have. Finally, the training and evaluation setup in this work depend on imperfect signals from which the method will inherit failure modes. For example, embedding-based diversity and deviation metrics may miss forms of creative variation, while LLM judges and reward models give imperfect quality signals. That said, better signals should directly improve the learned primer, so the outcomes can in principle improve along with its supporting technology.

7 Conclusion

This work identifies the creative paradox, the tension that training on past creative successes teaches a model to reproduce them, while true creativity demands moving beyond previous outputs. The proposed solution to get around the paradox is creative priming. Compared to directly training the response model, CP produces more responses that are simultaneously novel, high-quality, and semantically distinct. The deeper lesson is that if creativity is a process rather than an output, then optimizing the creative process itself, learning to generate better primers rather than better answers, is really where the discourse on optimizing for creativity should focus. We hope this work will inspire more discussion and investigation in this spirit.

Appendix A Algorithms

This section provides pseudocode algorithms for GRPO (Algorithm 1), creative priming (Algorithm 2), and DGRPO (Algorithm 3) along with additional details on the reward components.

A.1 GRPO

A.2 Creative Priming Training Algorithm

Algorithm 2 gives the full training loop for the creative priming model described in Section 3.1. It instantiates the standard GRPO loop (Algorithm 1) with the two-level primer/response sampling and the multiplicative Reward⁡(⋅)\mathrm{Reward}(\cdot) of Eq. 5.

No-deviation variant of CC.

In the variant trained without deviation (Section 3.3), the per-response score ckc_{k} (Eq. 7) drops the deviation factor Devk\mathrm{Dev}_{k}, and the response creativity CC (Eq. 8) reduces to the fraction of responses above the quality threshold,

Qfrac=1Gresp∑k=1Gresp{qk>T},∈[0,1].Q_{\mathrm{frac}}=\frac{1}{G_{\mathrm{resp}}}\sum_{k=1}^{G_{\mathrm{resp}}}\mathds{1}\!\left\{q_{k}>T\right\},\qquad\in[0,1]. (14)

A.3 Diversified GRPO (DGRPO)

This appendix gives the full training loop and reward specification for the Diversified GRPO (DGRPO) baseline introduced in Section 2.2.2. DGRPO trains the response model πresp\pi_{\mathrm{resp}} directly for diversity and quality. Here the response model is itself the policy: for each prompt a group of responses is sampled, each one scored, and πresp\pi_{\mathrm{resp}} is updated with GRPO (Algorithm 1). The only departure from a standard GRPO run is the reward, which is a pointwise, multiplicative combination of a per-response quality term and a per-response diversity term, optionally multiplied by a deviation term measured against a reference set of responses. Throughout, ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot) and the clipped cosine distance d⁡(a,b)\mathrm{d}(a,b) are as defined in Section 2.2.1.

A.3.1 Reward Components

Unlike a standard GRPO reward, which assigns a single scalar to each response in isolation, the response-model reward couples each response’s quality with how different it is from the others in its group (plus an optional deviation term). For the ii-th response of prompt XjX^{j}, the reward is

rj,i=Qi⏟quality⋅Di⏟diversity⋅[Devi]⏟optional.r_{j,i}=\;\underbrace{Q_{i}}_{\text{quality}}\cdot\underbrace{D_{i}}_{\text{diversity}}\cdot\underbrace{\big[\,\mathrm{Dev}_{i}\,\big]}_{\text{optional}}. (15)

Each factor is non-negative, so a response is rewarded only when it is simultaneously high quality, diverse from its siblings, and (when enabled) deviating from the reference model.

Intra-group diversity DiD_{i}.

This measure is the cosine distance of response ii to its siblings within the same group, using the cosine distance d⁡(⋅,⋅)\mathrm{d}(\cdot,\cdot):

Di=1G−1​∑i′≠id⁡(Yj,i,Yj,i′),∈[0,1].D_{i}=\frac{1}{G-1}\sum_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\mathrm{d}\!\left(Y^{j,i},Y^{j,i^{\prime}}\right),\qquad\in[0,1]. (16)

As an alternative to the embedding distance, a partition-based diversity can be applied (as in DARLING), in which a binary equivalence classifier groups the GG responses into semantic partitions and response ii receives Di=(G−|partition⁡(i)|)/(G−1)D_{i}=(G-|\mathrm{partition}(i)|)/(G-1), rewarding responses that fall in small (rare) partitions.

Quality QiQ_{i}.

This measure is a per-response quality score. One of two scorers computes the score, depending on the setting:

Qi={σ⁡(rRM​(Xj,Yj,i)−Tτ)(sigmoid reward model),rRM​(Xj,Yj,i)(raw reward model, DARLING).Q_{i}=\begin{cases}\sigma\!\left(\dfrac{r_{\mathrm{RM}}(X^{j},Y^{j,i})-T}{\tau}\right)&\text{(sigmoid reward model)},\\[10.0pt] r_{\mathrm{RM}}(X^{j},Y^{j,i})&\text{(raw reward model, DARLING)}.\end{cases} (17)

The sigmoid variant maps the raw reward-model score to [0,1][0,1] with the quality threshold TT as the inflection point and temperature τ\tau controlling sharpness, while the raw variant follows DARLING and uses the (unbounded) reward-model score directly.

Deviation Devi\mathrm{Dev}_{i} (optional).

Deviation of response ii relative to a set of reference responses ℛrefj={Yrefj,k}k\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{ref}}^{j}=\{Y_{\mathrm{ref}}^{j,k}\}_{k} sampled from a frozen reference model πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} for the same prompt gives this measure:

Devi=1Gref​∑Yref∈ℛrefjd⁡(Yj,i,Yref).\mathrm{Dev}_{i}=\frac{1}{G_{\mathrm{ref}}}\sum_{Y_{\mathrm{ref}}\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{ref}}^{j}}\mathrm{d}\!\left(Y^{j,i},Y_{\mathrm{ref}}\right). (18)

This pushes the trained policy’s responses away from what the (untrained) reference model would produce, encouraging exploration beyond the base distribution rather than mere within-group spread. When deviation is disabled, the term is omitted and the reward reduces to rj,i=Qi⋅Dir_{j,i}=Q_{i}\cdot D_{i}.

Appendix B Penalty-based creative primer judge

Throughout the main paper, the creative primer judge JCPJ_{\mathrm{CP}} is the criterion-mean judge of Eq. 11: it scores a primer by the mean of five positive criteria (specificity, thinking strategy, content focus, prompt faithfulness, focus), setting the score to zero if the primer addresses the model in the third person rather than directly. Every result reported in the main paper uses this criterion-mean judge. Here, we study a penalty-based judge JCPpenaltyJ_{\mathrm{CP}}^{\mathrm{penalty}}, which embodies the opposite scoring philosophy. Rather than asking how good a primer is, it asks “does this primer exhibit any specific failure modes?” It flags a set of criteria 𝒥\mathcal{J}, and each criterion cc contributes a penalty pcp_{c} when triggered (gc∈{0,1}g_{c}\in\{0,1\}), starting from a perfect score of 100100:

JCPpenalty=1100​(100−∑c∈𝒥pc​gc),∈[0,1].J_{\mathrm{CP}}^{\mathrm{penalty}}=\frac{1}{100}\left(100-\sum_{c\in\mathcal{J}}p_{c}\,g_{c}\right),\qquad\in[0,1]. (19)

The criteria are weighted by severity. Three severe failure modes (pc=10p_{c}=10) target primers that fail at the basic job of guiding thinking: kitchen sink (piling on many unrelated strategies without a coherent through-line), meta-instructions (reading as advice about how to write a primer rather than being an actual primer), and style over substance (guiding only the output’s format, tone, or presentation instead of what to reason about). Four minor failure modes (pc=3p_{c}=3) target subtler defects: distorts intent (steering responses toward a meaningfully different question than the one asked, e.g. inviting fiction for a factual prompt), generic (advice so broad it could be prepended to any prompt, with no reference to this one’s specifics), dictates content (prescribing specific content or structure to produce rather than an angle to think from), and third-party reference (referring to the model in the third person, e.g. “the model should…”, instead of addressing it directly). Whereas the criterion-mean judge forces the entire score to zero when the primer fails to address the model directly, the penalty-based judge treats every violation as a soft deduction. A failed or unparseable judgment yields JCPpenalty=0J_{\mathrm{CP}}^{\mathrm{penalty}}=0.

Ablation.

To isolate the impact of each judge rubric, we train CP models with the only difference being the judge template (JCPJ_{\mathrm{CP}} vs. JCPpenaltyJ_{\mathrm{CP}}^{\mathrm{penalty}}), run the comparison both with and without a deviation reward, and show the full results in Table 3. The results show that the judge rubric makes a bigger difference when there is no deviation reward signal to directly drive creativity. Without a deviation term, replacing the criterion-mean judge with the penalty rubric reduces every creativity metric: filtered distinct clusters fall from 16.116.1 to 10.410.4, filtered Vendi from 4.044.04 to 3.063.06, deviation from 21.221.2 to 17.117.1, and VUS by a comparable margin. Because the penalty rubric only suppresses failure modes and never rewards substantive priming, the primer model converges on safe, clean, low-deviation primers that score well on quality but do little to diversify the responses. Once an explicit deviation reward is present, however, the deviation term directly rewards creativity and the judge choice becomes less impactful. The results from each rubric land within confidence intervals of each other on essentially every metric, with the criterion-mean judge slightly ahead on the filtered metrics and quality.

Appendix C Evaluation metrics

This appendix expands the description of evaluation metrics from Section 4.

Embedder.

All embedding-based evaluation metrics (deviation, diversity, and Vendi score) reuse the cosine distance d⁡(a,b)\mathrm{d}(a,b) from Section 2.2.1, computed on embeddings from jinaai/jina-embeddings-v5-text-small. We deliberately evaluate with a different embedder than the Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B model used to compute training rewards to avoid overfitting to any specific embedding model.

Vendi score.

The Vendi score (Friedman and Dieng, 2023) is the effective number of distinct responses in a set, computed as the exponential of the Shannon entropy of the eigenvalues of the normalized similarity matrix K/nK/n with Ki​j=1−d⁡(ai,aj)K_{ij}=1-\mathrm{d}(a_{i},a_{j}). It ranges from 11 (when all responses are identical) to nn (when all are mutually dissimilar) providing a soft, embedding-based counterpart to counting discrete distinct clusters.

Distinct clusters.

Following NoveltyBench (Zhang et al., 2025) and DARLING (Li et al., 2025), we count the semantic-equivalence clusters in a response set. The classifier released by NoveltyBench (a fine-tuned deberta-v3-large44 4 https://huggingface.co/yimingzhang/deberta-v3-large-generation-similarity) greedily partitions the set into these clusters, and we report the resulting cluster count.

Filtered spread (Vendi score and distinct clusters).

To measure the creativity of each method, we use a series of compound metrics that first filter the responses for individual creativity (simultaneous high-quality and deviation), and then measure spread over the survivors. We start with the filtered Vendi score and filtered distinct clusters which first keep only the individually creative responses (exceeding both a deviation and a quality threshold), and then measure Vendi score and distinct clusters over the surviving set. That way, spread is credited only among creative responses. We measure spread with the Vendi score rather than diversity because filtering leaves each method with a different number of survivors, and mean pairwise distance is biased against larger sets; for example, the diversity of a large set can only match that of a set of two if every one of its pairs is equally far apart. Counting effective distinct survivors instead lets us fairly compare methods that have different numbers of creative responses.

The compound metrics require thresholds for quality and deviation and we aim to devise principled thresholds for each. For the quality threshold, we set a separate threshold per prompt using the mean quality of the direct-generation reference set. That is to say, prompts for which direct generation achieves higher quality are assigned higher thresholds, while prompts for which it performs worse are assigned lower thresholds. The deviation threshold is set to 0.20.2 based on the findings of Jiang et al. (2025), who find that the average pairwise similarity among responses to the same prompt typically exceeds 0.80.8. Therefore, a response of at least 0.20.2 in cosine distance from the reference set falls outside the typical spread of the reference distribution, a reasonable starting point for treating it as unlikely to have come from the reference model.

Threshold sweeps: AUC and VUS.

However, even a well-motivated threshold is only one operating point, and the optimal threshold varies based on the application, where some settings prize rare outliers, and others require a high quality floor. For that reason, we include additional metrics that sweep thresholds across their operating range. Sweeping the deviation threshold and integrating the filtered metric over the sweep using the trapezoid rule gives an AUC-dev (illustrated in Figure 8); we report it for both filtered Vendi and filtered distinct clusters, and analogously report an AUC-qual from a swept quality threshold. Sweeping both thresholds jointly produces a surface over the deviation×\timesquality plane, whose volume under the surface (VUS) serves as a single threshold-free summary of system creativity, computed for filtered Vendi and, separately, filtered distinct clusters.

Appendix D API-model transfer: full results

Table 4 reports the complete API-model transfer results summarized in Figure 5, across the same atomic and compound metrics as Table 1, for both Creative Priming variants (trained without and with a deviation term) with confidence intervals. Each API model is evaluated against its own direct-generation reference. Every deviation-derived metric (deviation and all eight compound metrics) is measured relative to the direct responses and is therefore zero for each reference by construction, shown as “-”.

Appendix E Composing creative priming with verbalized sampling

Table 5 adds two new settings to the API-model transfer results of Table 4. The first is verbalized sampling (VS) (Zhang et al., 2026), a test-time prompting method in which the model generates multiple candidate responses, and tags each with a self-reported probability, and is instructed to sample from the tail of its own distribution. The second setting composes VS with creative priming: in this experiment, the primer generates 88 creative primers per prompt, and each primer is sent to the API model in a single verbalized-sampling call returning 88 responses. The VS setting issues 88 such calls of 88 responses each. Each method therefore generates 6464 completions per prompt. Only the deviation-trained primer is included in this experiment.

Verbalized Sampling reaches higher response diversity than CP (+ div.) for all four response models (29.829.8–33.333.3 versus 22.222.2–31.131.1), but its judge score falls below direct generation on both GPT models (83.283.2 versus 90.690.6 for GPT-5-nano and 85.285.2 versus 89.789.7 for GPT-5.4), while CP (+ div.) is above direct generation on all four. On the compound metrics, CP (+ div.) leads VS on all eight for both GPT models and on nearly all metrics for Sonnet-4.6. Only on Opus-4.8 do the methods split the compound metrics of creativity.

However, the composition of CP + VS performs the best on every compound metric for all four response models. VUS distinct clusters for Sonnet-4.6 reaches 1268.61268.6, against 664.8664.8 for CP (+ div.) and 540.1540.1 for VS, and filtered distinct clusters improves on the component parts by 1.41.4–3.1×3.1\times across the four response models.

Appendix F Impact of training on response style

A method that changes either how a model writes or what it says will both lead to increased embedding deviation, but changes to surface-level style are not the type of deviation that we want to encourage. Therefore, rather than relying entirely on the embedding model signals, we also calculate an explicit set of style features:

  • •

    Length: response length in tokens (using the shared Qwen3-8B response-model tokenizer) and mean sentence length in words. Together these separate terse output from flowing prose: a response can be long yet built from short fragments, or short yet written in long sentences.

  • •

    Formatting: the fraction of responses that use a Markdown header, bold span, or list. These capture structural presentation independent of wording.

  • •

    Stylometry: the Jensen-Shannon divergence (Lin, 1991) between a method’s pooled distribution over common function words and the reference’s. Function-word frequencies carry little topical content and have long served as an authorship fingerprint in stylometry (Mosteller and Wallace, 1963), so this distance isolates stylistic drift from topical change. It is measured at the method level (pooled over all responses) and so has no per-prompt interval.

For each feature we average its value over a prompt’s 64 responses, then average those per-prompt means across prompts, separately for each method and for the reference. Confidence intervals are 95% half-widths over the per-prompt means, matching the convention of Table 1. Table 6 reports the results.

The three methods land in three distinct style regimes. DGRPO becomes terse on every axis, cutting response length, sentence length, and nearly all formatting. DARLING moves the opposite way, lengthening responses and doubling list use, and it registers the largest function-word shift, indicating that much of its deviation is a change in style rather than content. CP shifts toward long-sentence prose (its sentences are the longest of any method while its responses are shorter than the reference) yet drifts least in function-word usage, so its deviation reflects a change in what is said more than in how it is written.

Figure 9 makes these regimes concrete on a single prompt. The reference names the obvious fighter and pads it with a blurb; DGRPO answers in one terse line; DARLING returns a bolded, bulleted analysis; and CP answers in flowing prose while naming a different fighter and framing its historical significance, illustrating that its deviation lies in what it says rather than in surface formatting.

Appendix G Additional qualitative examples

Figures 10, 11, 12, and 13 demonstrate, qualitatively, the most and least creative responses to four prompts. The prompts span a short story, a joke, a short factual request, and an open-ended question, illustrating how each method’s outputs vary with the type of prompt.

Appendix H DGRPO group-size scaling

Table 7 reports the complete results for the DGRPO group-size scaling experiment. The G=8 row corresponds to the primary experimental setting. The remaining runs scale deviation-trained DGRPO to G∈{16,32,64}G\in\{16,32,64\}, while the training data, two-epoch training horizon, and all other hyperparameters remain fixed. Increasing G gives DGRPO additional on-policy samples and therefore intentionally departs from the primary matched setting. At G=64, DGRPO samples the same number of responses per prompt as the 64 response-model generations that contribute to CP’s primer reward estimates. The sweep focuses on DGRPO because DARLING already trains for ten epochs, making group-size scaling substantially harder to interpret as a compute comparison.

Deviation increases monotonically across the sweep, while response diversity and Vendi score decline. Quality and distinct clusters fluctuate before reaching their lowest values at G=64. Every compound metric reaches its highest DGRPO value at G=32 and subsequently declines at G=64. Figure 4(b) provides a comparison with CP.

Appendix I DGRPO Ablation: reweighting quality

The atomic metrics in Table 1 show that training a response model directly forces a tradeoff between quality and the creativity axes: DGRPO attains the highest response diversity and deviation of any method trained with a deviation reward, but the lowest judge score (77.377.3, versus 90.590.5 for the reference). A natural question is whether this tradeoff is an artifact of how DGRPO’s multiplicative reward (Eq. 15) balances its terms and whether simply weighting quality more heavily can recover quality without sacrificing diversity.

We generalize the DGRPO reward with a per-term exponent weight,

rj,i=QiwQ⋅DiwD⋅DeviwDev.r_{j,i}=Q_{i}^{\,w_{Q}}\cdot D_{i}^{\,w_{D}}\cdot\mathrm{Dev}_{i}^{\,w_{\mathrm{Dev}}}. (20)

Because Qi,Di,Devi∈[0,1]Q_{i},D_{i},\mathrm{Dev}_{i}\in[0,1] (Eqs. 16–18), an exponent w>1w>1 effectively penalizes lower values more aggressively than higher values. We hold wD=wDev=1w_{D}=w_{\mathrm{Dev}}=1 and sweep the quality exponent wQ∈{1.0,1.2,1.5,2.0}w_{Q}\in\{1.0,1.2,1.5,2.0\}, retraining DGRPO from scratch at each setting and evaluating on NoveltyBench. The wQ=1.0w_{Q}=1.0 row is the DGRPO (+Deviation) model from Table 1.

Increasing the quality exponent does not resolve the tradeoff (Table 8). Across wQ∈[1.0,2.0]w_{Q}\in[1.0,2.0], the judge score stays within a narrow 76.576.5–80.180.1 band—never approaching the reference’s 90.590.5—while response diversity, deviation, and distinct clusters are essentially unchanged (all differences fall within overlapping confidence intervals). The compound creativity metrics move only marginally, peaking weakly at wQ=1.5w_{Q}=1.5. Reweighting quality therefore has little leverage on DGRPO’s quality–creativity balance.

Appendix J DARLING across training epochs

In the main work, DARLING is trained following the original recipe of 10 epochs (Li et al., 2025), compared to the 2 epochs used for DGRPO and CP. To rule out the possibility that this longer schedule either harms or advantages DARLING relative to the other methods, we evaluate its checkpoints at every 2 epochs (2, 4, 6, 8, 10). The 2-epoch checkpoint is the equal-data-budget comparison against DGRPO and CP, and the 10-epoch rows are the same as the DARLING rows of Table 1.

At the equal-data budget of 2 epochs, DARLING is no more creative than at its reported 10-epoch checkpoint; without the deviation reward its simple diversity peaks around epochs 4–6 and then declines as continued training trades diversity for reward-model quality. However, we do see deviation increasing throughout training. In all cases DARLING’s compound creativity metrics remain far below those of CP (Table 1), so the epoch mismatch neither advantages nor explains away the gap: DARLING does not become competitive at any point along its training trajectory.

Appendix K Templates

This appendix collects the prompt templates used throughout this work. Figure 14 shows the template that elicits a creative primer from the primer model used in evaluation (1 of 32 used during training), Figure 15 gives the template that conditions the response model on that primer, and Figure 16 gives the template used by the creative primer judge JCPJ_{\mathrm{CP}} (Eq. 11). Figures 17–19 give the LLM-as-a-judge template used for response-quality evaluation: this judge scores every response on six fixed universal components and on a set of prompt-specific components that are generated once per prompt at annotation time. Figure 17 shows the template skeleton with its three placeholders left unfilled, and Figures 18 and 19 show the prompt-specific components materialized for two example prompts from NoveltyBench.
